name: Lemongrass

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lemongrass grows best in a moist, rich, well-drained loam with high organic content. As a fast-growing grass it is a heavy user of both nutrients and water, so a fertile soil amended generously with compost supports the vigorous clump growth that produces thick, harvestable stalks. Good drainage matters despite the high water demand: soils that stay waterlogged invite root rot. The plant tolerates a range of soil types, so the practical goal is a soil that holds moisture and feeds well while still draining freely.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Give lemongrass rich, moist soil that has been improved with plenty of compost. It is a hungry, thirsty grass, so the better the soil, the bigger the clump. Make sure the spot still drains, because soil that stays soggy can rot the roots.

ph.note_seasoned: Lemongrass is not fussy about pH and tolerates a wide range of soils. A preferred range of 6.0 to 7.5 keeps the full spectrum of nutrients available to this fast-growing, nutrient-hungry grass, and it will grow acceptably in mildly acidic through mildly alkaline ground. No specific pH figure is published in the Tier-1 extension guides consulted, so this range is modeled from the plant's documented tolerance of varied soils and from general practice for culinary grasses.
ph.note_beginner: Lemongrass is easygoing about soil pH. Aim for roughly 6.0 to 7.5, which is ordinary garden soil, and you will not need to make any special adjustment.

fertilizer.timing: Weekly to every other week through the active summer growing season; ease off as fall approaches
fertilizer.example_product: balanced soluble fertilizer at half strength (as recommended for lemongrass), or a nitrogen-forward all-purpose liquid
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Like other grasses, lemongrass is a heavy nitrogen feeder, and steady feeding drives the vigorous leaf and stalk growth that makes a productive clump. Utah State Extension recommends feeding weekly with a half-strength solution of a balanced soluble fertilizer from June through September; a nitrogen-forward all-purpose liquid every one to two weeks works similarly. Container plants need more frequent feeding than in-ground clumps because nutrients leach with each watering. Taper feeding as fall approaches so growth is not pushed into cold weather.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Lemongrass is a hungry grass and grows fastest when fed often. Use a liquid fertilizer at about half strength every week or two through the summer. If it is in a pot, feed a bit more often, since watering washes nutrients out. Stop feeding as fall nears.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to feed your lemongrass. Grasses are heavy nitrogen users; apply a balanced soluble fertilizer at half strength, or a nitrogen-forward all-purpose liquid, every one to two weeks through the summer growing season. Feed container plants a little more often.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your lemongrass could use a feed. Mix a liquid fertilizer to about half the label strength and water it in at the base. Do this every week or two through summer, a bit more often for pots.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Nitrogen-forward; a balanced soluble at half strength or a higher-first-number all-purpose liquid keeps this fast-growing grass in vigorous leaf
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a general-purpose feed higher in the first number (nitrogen)
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Half-strength soluble fertilizer weekly through summer; more frequent for containers as nutrients leach
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Half the label strength, every week or two through summer

pests.name: Generally pest-resistant (aromatic-oil deterrence)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Healthy in-ground lemongrass rarely shows insect damage. Extension guides describe it as essentially free of pest problems when grown well, an effect attributed to the citral-rich essential oils in its foliage that repel many insects. Scattered chewing or a few sap-feeders may appear on stressed or crowded plants but seldom rise to a real infestation outdoors.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lemongrass is one of the least pest-troubled herbs you can grow. Its own lemony oils keep most bugs away, so outdoor plants usually look clean.
pests.cause_seasoned: The plant's aromatic oils (notably citral) are used in insect-repellent products. Robust, well-watered clumps in full sun are the least attractive to pests; stress and crowding are what invite occasional trouble.
pests.cause_beginner: Lemongrass makes lemony oils that many insects dislike, so it is naturally left alone. Keeping it healthy and unstressed keeps it that way.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rarely needed outdoors. For the occasional sap-feeder, a strong jet of water or an insecticidal soap spray is sufficient. Remove and destroy badly damaged outer leaves. Improving airflow and vigor usually resolves minor issues without any product.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You will seldom need to treat lemongrass. If you do see a few bugs, blast them off with water or use an insecticidal soap. Trim off any damaged leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow in full sun with rich soil and steady water to keep clumps vigorous, and divide crowded clumps so air moves through them. Vigorous plants are the best defense.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep lemongrass healthy with sun, rich soil, and plenty of water, and divide it when it gets crowded. A strong plant rarely has pest trouble.

pests.name: Spider mites (indoor and hot, dry conditions)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or a dusty, faded look on the leaf blades, sometimes with delicate webbing where the leaf meets the stem, most often on plants overwintered indoors or grown in hot, dry, stagnant air. Heavy feeding bronzes and dries the foliage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny specks and a faded, dusty look on the leaves, sometimes with fine webbing. This shows up mostly on plants kept indoors over winter.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spider mites (Tetranychidae) thrive in the warm, dry, low-airflow conditions of a heated indoor room, which is exactly where potted lemongrass spends the winter. They are far less of a problem on well-watered outdoor clumps.
pests.cause_beginner: Spider mites are tiny pests that love warm, dry indoor air. They tend to appear on lemongrass that is overwintering inside.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse the foliage with a strong spray of water, raise humidity around indoor plants, and treat persistent infestations with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, covering the leaf undersides. Cutting the plant back hard before bringing it indoors reduces the mite population it carries in.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water to knock mites off and raise the humidity around indoor plants. For stubborn cases, use insecticidal soap. Cutting the plant back before bringing it inside helps a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Before overwintering, cut the plant back and inspect it, and keep indoor humidity up with misting or a nearby water tray. Avoid hot, dry, stagnant spots for indoor pots.
pests.prevention_beginner: Before bringing lemongrass indoors, trim it back and check it over. Keep the indoor air from getting too hot and dry by misting now and then.

diseases.name: Lemongrass rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small chlorotic (yellow) flecks appear on both leaf surfaces and enlarge into reddish to crimson streaks; on the leaf underside these rupture into powdery orange-brown pustules. Severe infection produces large patches of tan to purplish dead tissue and dries the leaves, cutting yield and quality. It is favored by warm, humid weather and crowded, poorly ventilated plantings.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow flecks that turn into reddish streaks, plus orange-brown powdery spots on the undersides of the leaves. Bad cases dry the leaves out. It shows up most in warm, humid, crowded conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Rust caused by the fungus Puccinia nakanishikii, the most notable disease of lemongrass in humid tropical and subtropical areas; the University of Hawaii CTAHR documents it, and it has been reported on Florida lemongrass. Spores spread on wind and splashing water, and dense, wet, still canopies favor infection.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called rust, spread by wind and splashing water. It is most common where it is warm, humid, and the plants are packed close together.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves to reduce spore load, and open the clump up by dividing and thinning to improve airflow. Water at the base rather than overhead so leaves dry quickly. Copper-based fungicides can be used preventively where rust pressure is high; culture is the primary control.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and throw away badly spotted leaves, and thin or divide crowded clumps so air moves through. Water at the base, not over the leaves. A copper fungicide can help if rust is a recurring problem.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space and divide clumps for good air movement, water at the soil line to keep foliage dry, and avoid overhead irrigation in humid weather. Vigorous, uncrowded plants in full sun resist rust best.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room, divide crowded clumps, and water at the base so the leaves stay dry. Good airflow and full sun are the best prevention.

diseases.name: Leaf blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown, elongated lesions develop along the leaf blades in warm, wet weather and can spread quickly through dense plantings, browning and drying the foliage from the tips and margins inward.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown streaks and dead patches on the leaves during warm, wet spells. In crowded plants it can spread fast.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A foliar leaf-blight fungus that is favored by prolonged leaf wetness, high humidity, and crowding. As with rust, still, wet canopies drive it, and it is the second disease of note for lemongrass grown in humid regions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A leaf fungus that thrives when leaves stay wet and plants are packed together in warm, humid weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves, thin or divide crowded clumps, and switch to base watering to shorten leaf-wetness periods. Copper-based products can be used preventively under heavy pressure.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Trim off the blighted leaves, thin crowded clumps, and water at the base instead of over the top. A copper spray can help in bad cases.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prioritize airflow (wide spacing, regular division) and dry foliage (base watering, morning irrigation). Avoid working in or harvesting from wet plants, which spreads spores.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep plants spaced and divided so air moves through, and water at the base so leaves dry fast. Try not to handle the plants while they are wet.

diseases.name: Root rot (overwatering in poor drainage)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, and collapse of stalks despite wet soil, with soft, dark, decayed roots and stalk bases. It appears when a thirsty plant is grown in soil that stays waterlogged, especially in containers with poor drainage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant yellows, wilts, and rots at the base even though the soil is wet. The roots turn soft and dark. This comes from soil that stays soggy.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Although lemongrass demands abundant water, its roots rot in soil that is chronically waterlogged. Soil-borne rot organisms take hold when drainage is poor or a pot sits in standing water, so drainage is as important as watering volume.
diseases.cause_beginner: Lemongrass loves water but hates sitting in it. If the soil or pot does not drain, the roots rot.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once roots are extensively rotted; remove affected plants. Improve drainage, repot into a free-draining mix, empty saucers after watering, and water generously but allow excess to drain freely.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save a badly rotted plant, so remove it. Fix the drainage, repot into fresh mix if it is in a container, and never let the pot sit in standing water.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil; in containers use a free-draining mix and pots with ample holes, and empty the saucer after each watering. Water deeply and often, but let the excess escape.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow lemongrass in soil or a pot that drains well. Water it a lot, but make sure the extra water can run out and the pot never sits in a full saucer.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Frequently through the warm season; in-ground clumps deeply 2-3 times per week in heat, containers often daily
watering.frequency_beginner: Water often. In the ground, water deeply a few times a week in hot weather; in a pot, check daily and do not let it dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Keep the root zone consistently moist; this is a high-water-demand grass, so err toward generous, deep watering while ensuring drainage
watering.amount_beginner: Keep the soil consistently moist, never bone dry. Lemongrass drinks a lot.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base by hand or flood irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers; keeping the foliage dry limits rust and leaf blight, and base watering suits this thirsty grass. In containers, water until it drains from the bottom and empty the saucer.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, to help prevent leaf diseases. In a pot, water until it runs out the bottom, then empty the saucer.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing and wilting despite wet soil, soft dark stalk bases, and a soured, waterlogged root zone signal root rot from poor drainage rather than too little water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Yellow, wilting leaves and a soft, dark base even though the soil is wet mean the roots are sitting in water. Improve the drainage.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Leaf tips and margins browning and curling, slowed clump expansion, and thin, slow-forming stalks indicate the plant is not getting enough water, especially during hot, dry spells.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Browning, curling leaf tips and slow growth mean it is thirsty. Lemongrass wilts and browns quickly when it runs short of water.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: A newly set-out division or rooted start needs consistently moist soil to establish its roots; do not let it dry out during the first few weeks.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep a new plant's soil moist while it settles in. Do not let it dry out.

schedule_by_stage.frequency: 2-3 times per week in-ground; daily for containers in heat
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: This is the main growth phase, when heat and water drive rapid clump expansion. Water deeply and often, ensuring drainage.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: During the hot growing months, water deeply and often. This is when the clump bulks up.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Maintain generous, consistent moisture as stalks thicken to harvestable size; water stress thins the stalks.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering well as the stalks fatten up. Dry spells make thin stalks.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep moisture steady through the harvest period to sustain continued stalk production from the clump.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering as you harvest so the clump keeps making new stalks.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Lemongrass has an unusually high water demand for an herb, yet it still needs sharp drainage. The reconciling rule is to water deeply and frequently while never letting the root zone stagnate. Watering at the base or by flood irrigation, rather than overhead, both suits the plant and keeps foliage dry to limit rust and leaf blight.
watering.method_note_beginner: Lemongrass drinks more than most herbs but hates soggy roots. Water it deeply and often, at the base, and make sure the extra water drains away.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The first few weeks after planting (root establishment) and the peak heat of summer, when a fast-growing clump can dry out quickly, are the moments water stress does the most damage.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water most carefully right after planting and during the hottest part of summer, when the plant dries out fastest.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Lemongrass is almost always started from a division of an existing clump, from a nursery transplant, or by rooting a fresh grocery-store stalk (leaves and roots removed) in a glass of water, where roots form in about two to three weeks. Seed is possible but slow and rarely used. Start or pot up divisions indoors roughly 8 weeks before the last frost to have a well-rooted plant ready to set out. Transplant outdoors only after all frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed, and harden plants off over several days first. It grows slowly until summer heat arrives, then bulks up dramatically.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to start lemongrass is from a division or a nursery plant, or by standing a fresh grocery-store stalk in a glass of water until it grows roots (about two to three weeks), then potting it up. Get it going indoors about 8 weeks before your last frost, then set it outside once frost is past and the soil is warm. Ease it into the outdoors over a few days first. It stays small until summer heat kicks in, then takes off.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Whole fresh stalks keep for several days to about a week at cool room temperature. For anything longer, refrigerate or freeze. The tough stalks are far more durable than tender leafy herbs.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Fresh stalks last a few days to a week on the counter. For longer storage, use the fridge or freezer.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Wrapped loosely or sealed in a bag, fresh stalks keep 2 to 3 weeks in the refrigerator. Unlike basil, lemongrass has no chilling-injury problem and refrigerates well.
storage.fridge_beginner: Lemongrass keeps well in the fridge, about 2 to 3 weeks, wrapped or in a bag. Cold does not hurt it the way it does basil.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Lemongrass freezes excellently and is the best way to keep a large harvest. Freeze whole trimmed stalks, or slice or mince the tender bases and freeze in bags or portioned in ice cube trays; frozen stalks keep their flavor for many months. Leaves can be dried for tea.
storage.freezer_beginner: Lemongrass freezes very well. Freeze whole stalks or chop the tender part and freeze it in bags. It keeps its flavor for months. Dry the leaves for tea.
storage.notes_seasoned: Lemongrass stores far more easily than delicate leafy herbs: the stalks are fibrous and sturdy, refrigerate for weeks, and freeze for months with little flavor loss. Trim the leafy tops and peel tough outer layers before storing the tender stalk base you cook with. The cut leaves dry well for tea.
storage.notes_beginner: Lemongrass is easy to store. Keep stalks in the fridge for a couple of weeks or freeze them for months. Trim the tops and peel the tough outer layers off the part you cook with. Dry the leaves for tea.

recommended.name: West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus)
recommended.note: The common culinary lemongrass, of Malaysian origin, grown for its thick, tender edible stalks; this is the type sold as grocery-store lemongrass and the one to grow for cooking.

recommended.name: East Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon flexuosus)
recommended.note: Also called Cochin or Malabar grass. Native to India, Sri Lanka, Burma, and Thailand; also culinary and a major source of lemongrass essential oil, with somewhat more slender stalks.

recommended.name: Citronella grass (Cymbopogon nardus / C. winterianus)
recommended.note: A related but non-culinary species grown for citronella oil and as an ornamental insect-repellent plant; do not confuse it with edible lemongrass for cooking.

varieties.note_seasoned: For cooking, grow West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus), the species with the plump, tender stalk bases used in kitchens and the one usually sold fresh in stores. East Indian lemongrass (C. flexuosus) is also edible and is the main oil-crop species, with more slender stalks. The genus Cymbopogon holds dozens of species, and it is worth knowing that citronella grass (C. nardus and C. winterianus), the source of citronella oil, is a close relative that looks similar but is grown for repellent oil and ornament, not for eating. When buying a plant or a rooting stalk for the kitchen, confirm it is C. citratus.
varieties.note_beginner: For cooking, choose West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus), the kind sold in grocery stores with the thick, tender stalks. There is also East Indian lemongrass (C. flexuosus), which is edible too and used for oil. Watch out for citronella grass, a lookalike relative grown to make citronella oil and to repel bugs, not for eating. If you want to cook with it, make sure you are getting C. citratus.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lemongrass shares tomatoes' love of heat, full sun, and steady water, and its strong citrus oils are a traditional insect deterrent, so gardeners often tuck a clump at the corner of a warm-season bed. Give it room, since a mature clump is large.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Lemongrass essential oils (citral, geraniol) are well documented as insect repellents, and it is a common companion-planting recommendation for warm-season vegetable beds, but I found no Tier-1 extension trial measuring a lemongrass companion effect on tomato. Labeled traditional/low: sound shared-conditions rationale plus a real repellent mechanism, but no crop-specific measurement on this pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lemongrass and tomatoes both want heat, sun, and regular water, so they make easy neighbors. Lemongrass's strong lemony scent is a traditional way to help keep some insects away. Just give the grass its own space, because it grows into a big clump.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Peppers
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Peppers want the same heat, sun, and moisture as lemongrass and mature on a similar warm-season schedule, so they share a bed comfortably. The grass's aromatic oils are a traditional pest deterrent for the planting.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shared warm-season culture makes peppers a low-risk neighbor, and lemongrass's documented aromatic-oil repellency is the usual rationale for pairing it near vegetables. No Tier-1 lemongrass-pepper trial found, so traditional/low by close analogy and a real mechanism rather than a measured pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Peppers love the same heat and sun as lemongrass, so they grow well side by side. The grass's lemony scent may help keep some bugs off. Give the clump room to spread out.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Shade-loving, moisture-shy herbs (rosemary, sage, thyme)
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs want lean, dry, sharply drained soil, while lemongrass wants rich ground and constant moisture, so the two pull a shared bed in opposite directions. Keep the drought-tolerant herbs in their own drier spot.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: A genuine cultural-conditions conflict rather than folklore: lemongrass requires rich, evenly moist soil and heavy feeding, whereas Mediterranean subshrubs prefer lean, dry, fast-draining soil. Co-planting forces a watering and fertility compromise that disadvantages one side. Mechanistic/medium because the incompatibility is a management fact, not a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Herbs like rosemary, sage, and thyme want dry, lean soil, which is the opposite of what thirsty lemongrass needs. If you plant them together, one will always be unhappy. Give the dry-loving herbs their own spot and let lemongrass have the rich, well-watered ground it likes.

companions.note_seasoned: Lemongrass has little formal companion-planting research behind it, but two practical points hold up. First, its essential oils (rich in citral) are documented insect repellents, which is the basis for the tradition of planting it near warm-season vegetables such as tomatoes and peppers; treat the pest-deterrent benefit as traditional rather than proven at garden scale. Second, its cultural needs are the deciding factor in placement: it demands rich soil, heavy feeding, full sun, and abundant water, so it pairs naturally with other heat-loving, well-watered crops and conflicts with lean, dry-soil Mediterranean herbs. Give a mature clump ample room, since it reaches 3 to 6 feet.
companions.note_beginner: Lemongrass grows happily next to other sun-and-water lovers like tomatoes and peppers, and its lemony scent is a traditional way to discourage some insects. Keep it away from dry-soil herbs like rosemary and sage, which want the opposite conditions. Remember that lemongrass becomes a big clump, so give it plenty of space.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Empty the saucer after each watering; despite its thirst, lemongrass rots if its roots sit in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: After watering, empty the saucer under the pot. Lemongrass drinks a lot but its roots rot if left standing in water.

soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost for extra richness
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A rich, moisture-retentive but free-draining potting mix, ideally amended with compost for fertility
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost for fertility; this heavy feeder benefits from an organically rich mix that still drains freely

container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Container lemongrass dries out fast and needs frequent, generous watering, often daily in summer heat; water until it drains from the bottom and never let the pot stand in water.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out fast, so check container lemongrass daily in summer and water until it drains out the bottom.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container plants more often than in-ground clumps, since frequent watering leaches nutrients; a half-strength soluble feed every week through active growth suits them.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed pot-grown lemongrass a bit more often, about weekly at half strength, because watering flushes out the nutrients.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: In any zone that frosts, a container is the standard way to carry lemongrass over winter. Before the first fall frost, cut the plant back hard (to roughly 4 to 6 inches, which also sheds pests) and bring the pot to the brightest indoor spot available; a large clump can be divided down to a smaller pot first. Kept in bright light, watered less, and unfed through winter, it holds until spring, when it can go back outside after frost. This is also how gardeners in cold zones keep a favorite plant going year to year rather than buying new each spring.
overwintering.approach_beginner: To keep lemongrass over winter, grow it in a pot. Before the first frost, cut it back to a few inches and move the pot to your sunniest indoor window. Water it less and do not feed it through winter. When frost is past in spring, put it back outside. This lets you keep the same plant year after year.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Lemongrass is an excellent container plant, and in cold regions a pot is the practical way to grow it, because it can be moved indoors before frost. Use a large pot (at least 3 gallons, ideally 5 or more) to support the vigorous clump, with ample drainage holes and a rich, free-draining mix. The main tradeoffs of container culture are water and feeding: pots dry and leach faster than ground soil, so both must be more frequent. A potted clump outgrows its container within a season or two and benefits from spring division.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Lemongrass grows very well in a big pot, which is the easiest way to grow it in cold areas since you can bring it inside for winter. Use a large pot (5 gallons is great) with good drainage and rich mix. Water and feed pots more often than ground plants. Divide the clump in spring when it fills the pot.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers suit this high-water-demand grass well, keeping the reservoir topped up during hot weather. Ensure the mix wicks moisture without becoming waterlogged, and let the reservoir draw down periodically to keep the roots healthy.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots work well for thirsty lemongrass. Just let the water reservoir run low now and then so the roots do not stay soaked.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: As a long-lived perennial clump, lemongrass is not part of an annual rotation; it holds its spot for years and is renewed by division rather than replanted each season. If starting a new clump, simply choose a sunny, rich, well-drained site.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Lemongrass is a perennial that stays in one place for years, so you do not rotate it like an annual vegetable. Just give a new clump a sunny, rich, well-drained spot.
rotation.good_after: Any well-drained, fertile, sunny site (perennial; not rotated annually)
rotation.note_seasoned: Lemongrass belongs to the true grass family, Poaceae, unrelated to the mints, carrots, or nightshades of a typical vegetable rotation. Because it is a perennial clump held for several years and divided to renew, it sits outside the annual crop-rotation cycle. The practical placement rule is simply full sun, rich soil, and good drainage; every few years, lift and divide the clump to keep the center vigorous.
rotation.note_beginner: Lemongrass is a grass that lives for years in one spot, so you do not move it around each season like a vegetable. Plant it in a sunny, rich, well-drained place and divide the clump every few years to keep it strong.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A newly set-out division or rooted start settling in: leaves may look tired for a week or two, then new green blades begin pushing from the center as roots take hold. Growth is slow in cool weather and accelerates as the soil warms.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Your new plant getting established. It may look a little limp at first, then start sending up fresh green blades from the middle once its roots catch on.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the soil consistently moist while roots establish, and site the plant in full sun. Do not feed heavily yet. Protect from any late chill; do not set out until frost is safely past and soil is warm.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep it watered and in full sun while it settles in. Hold off on heavy feeding for now, and make sure cold nights are behind you.

growth_stages.name: Vegetative growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid clump expansion once summer heat arrives: many new tillers (shoots) fan out from the base, and the clump widens and thickens noticeably week to week. This is the heavy feeding and watering phase.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fast growth once it gets hot. The clump fills out with lots of new shoots and gets bigger every week.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply and often and feed regularly with a nitrogen-forward soluble fertilizer to drive clump growth. Ensure full sun; shaded plants make few, thin stalks.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water a lot and feed often through the summer to grow a big clump. Make sure it gets full sun, or it will make only a few thin stalks.

growth_stages.name: Mature clump
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Individual stalks swelling to about half an inch thick at the base, the signal that they are ready to harvest. The clump stands 3 to 6 feet tall in good conditions, with dense, aromatic foliage.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Stalks getting about half an inch thick at the bottom, which means they are ready to cut. The plant is now a tall, full clump.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin harvesting the thickest outer stalks while keeping moisture and feeding steady so the clump keeps producing. In cold zones, plan the pre-frost lift or final harvest.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Start cutting the thickest outer stalks. Keep watering and feeding so more keep coming. If you get frost, plan to dig it up or harvest it all before then.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A productive clump yielding harvestable stalks continuously through the warm season. Outer stalks are firm and thick; the clump refills from the center as you take from the edges.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A clump you can keep cutting from all season. Take the outer stalks and the middle keeps making new ones.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest outer stalks as needed by twisting and pulling or cutting at ground level; leave the clump intact to keep producing. Maintain water and feeding. Before fall frost, harvest heavily and lift or pot the plant to overwinter.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut outer stalks whenever you need them, leaving the clump to regrow. Keep it watered and fed. Before frost, harvest a lot and bring the plant indoors in a pot if you want to keep it.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start or pot up lemongrass now
notifications.body_seasoned: Pot up a division, nursery start, or a grocery-store stalk rooted in water about 8 weeks before your last frost, so you have a well-rooted plant to set out. Keep it warm and bright indoors. Do not move it outside until frost is past and the soil has warmed.
notifications.body_beginner: Start your lemongrass indoors now, about 8 weeks before your last frost. You can root a fresh grocery stalk in a glass of water, then pot it up. Keep it warm and bright. Do not put it outside until frost is over and the soil is warm.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed: harden off and plant out lemongrass
notifications.title_beginner: Frost is over: time to plant lemongrass outside
notifications.body_seasoned: With frost danger past and the soil warming, harden off the plant over several days and set it in full sun in rich, well-drained soil. Space clumps 2 to 3 feet apart. Water in well and keep the soil moist while it establishes.
notifications.body_beginner: Now that frost is done, ease the plant into the outdoors over a few days, then plant it in a sunny, rich spot with room to grow (2 to 3 feet). Water it well and keep the soil moist while it settles in.

notifications.title_seasoned: Begin regular feeding as lemongrass takes off
notifications.body_seasoned: As summer heat drives rapid growth, feed weekly to every other week with a nitrogen-forward soluble fertilizer at half strength and water deeply and often. This is a heavy-feeding, thirsty grass; consistent food and water build a big, productive clump.
notifications.body_beginner: Now that it is growing fast, feed it every week or two with a liquid fertilizer at half strength, and water deeply and often. The more you feed and water, the bigger the clump.

notifications.title_beginner: Your lemongrass is ready to harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Once stalks reach about half an inch thick at the base, start harvesting the thickest outer ones by twisting and pulling or cutting at ground level. Leave the clump intact so it keeps producing through the season.
notifications.body_beginner: When the stalks are about half an inch thick at the bottom, start cutting the thickest outer ones. Leave the rest of the clump to keep growing.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost approaching: harvest and overwinter lemongrass
notifications.title_beginner: Frost is coming: harvest and save your lemongrass
notifications.body_seasoned: Frost will kill the top growth, so harvest generously now. To keep the plant, cut it back hard, dig and pot the clump (or a division of it), and move it to a bright indoor spot before the first frost. In frost-free zones, no action is needed.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost will kill the leaves, so harvest a lot now. To save the plant, cut it back, dig it up into a pot, and bring it to a bright window before frost hits. If you never get frost, you can leave it be.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning: protect or harvest lemongrass
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost tonight: cover, bring in, or harvest lemongrass
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Lemongrass is killed to the ground by frost. Bring containers indoors immediately. For in-ground clumps, harvest what you can and, if you want to keep the plant, dig and pot a division before the freeze. Frost cloth offers only slight protection and will not save it from a hard freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost kills lemongrass. Bring pots inside tonight. For plants in the ground, harvest what you can, and dig up a piece into a pot if you want to keep it. A cover helps only a little against a hard freeze.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Lemongrass is damaged as temperatures fall toward 40 °F, even without a frost. Growth stalls and foliage can discolor. Bring containers into shelter and, in cold zones, plan to move the plant indoors for the season if nights are trending cold.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Lemongrass gets hurt when it drops toward 40 °F, even without frost. Move pots to a sheltered or indoor spot, and if cold nights are here to stay, bring it inside for the winter.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat wave: keep lemongrass well watered
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Lemongrass loves heat and keeps growing vigorously in a heat wave; it has no heat pause. The one risk is drying out, since a fast-growing clump uses water quickly. Water more deeply and often, especially container plants, and keep the root zone moist.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Lemongrass thrives in heat, so no need to worry about the temperature itself. Just keep it watered. In a heat wave it drinks fast, so water more often, especially pots.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Prolonged humidity: watch for rust and leaf blight
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Humid, wet spell: check lemongrass leaves
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid, still conditions and prolonged leaf wetness favor lemongrass rust and leaf blight, especially in crowded clumps. Water at the base, avoid overhead irrigation, and divide or thin dense clumps to improve airflow. Remove any spotted or streaked leaves.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Long warm, humid, wet spells can bring on leaf diseases, especially in crowded plants. Water at the base, not over the leaves, thin or divide crowded clumps, and snip off any spotted leaves.

establishment.text_seasoned: The simplest way to start lemongrass is to root a fresh grocery-store stalk: remove any leaves, stand the bare stalk in a glass of water in a bright spot, refresh the water every couple of days, and roots form in about two to three weeks. Pot it up once roots are an inch or two long. A nursery plant or a division from a friend's clump works just as well.
establishment.text_beginner: You can grow lemongrass from a stalk bought at the store. Stand it in a glass of water on a bright windowsill, change the water every few days, and in two to three weeks it grows roots. Then plant it in a pot. A nursery plant works too.

establishment.text_seasoned: Do not rush lemongrass outdoors. It is fully frost-tender and slows or stalls as temperatures approach 40 °F, so wait until all frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed before setting it out, and harden it off over several days first. Plants set out too early into cold soil simply sit and sulk.
establishment.text_beginner: Do not put lemongrass outside too early. It hates cold, so wait until frost is completely past and the soil is warm. Ease it into the outdoors over a few days first. Planting it out into cold ground just makes it stall.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Lemongrass is a grass, and like a lawn it is a heavy nitrogen feeder that rewards generous water. Feed a nitrogen-forward soluble fertilizer at half strength every week or two through summer and water deeply and often. The combination of heat, food, and water is what turns a small start into a 3-to-6-foot clump in a single season.
vegetative.text_beginner: Lemongrass is a grass, so it is hungry and thirsty like a lawn. Feed it a half-strength liquid fertilizer every week or two and water it a lot through summer. Heat plus food plus water grows a big clump fast.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Site lemongrass in full sun. It is emphatically not shade-tolerant: in shade it makes only a few thin stalks and can decline outright. Give it the hottest, brightest spot you have, and it will reward you with a dense, vigorous clump.
vegetative.text_beginner: Give lemongrass full sun. In shade it makes just a few skinny stalks and may fade away. Put it in the hottest, sunniest spot you have.

mature.text_seasoned: Harvest as soon as stalks reach about half an inch thick at the base; you do not need to wait for the end of the season. Take the thickest outer stalks and leave the clump intact, and it will keep sending up new ones. Harvesting the outside actually keeps the clump vigorous.
mature.text_beginner: You can start cutting once stalks are about half an inch thick at the bottom, anytime in the season. Take the fat outer stalks and leave the rest; the clump keeps making more.

harvest.text_seasoned: To harvest, grasp an outer stalk low down, push it to the side, and twist and pull it free at the base, or cut it at ground level with a knife. Trim off the grassy top, peel away the tough outer layers, and use the tender inner base for cooking. Save the fragrant leaves to dry for tea.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick a stalk from the outside of the clump: push it sideways and twist and pull it off at the base, or cut it at ground level. Cut off the leafy top, peel off the tough outer layers, and use the tender white part in cooking. Dry the leaves for tea.

harvest.text_seasoned: Lemongrass stores easily. Whole stalks keep 2 to 3 weeks in the refrigerator, and the tender bases freeze for months with little flavor loss, sliced or whole. Before the first frost in cold zones, do a big final harvest and freeze the surplus, then lift and pot the clump to overwinter indoors.
harvest.text_beginner: Lemongrass keeps well. Stalks last a couple of weeks in the fridge and freeze for months. Before frost, harvest a big batch and freeze what you cannot use, then bring the plant indoors in a pot for winter.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single well-grown clump in full sun with rich soil and steady water can, by late summer, yield dozens of harvestable stalks and a steady supply through the season, plus abundant leaves for tea. In a frost-free climate an established perennial clump becomes a large, ongoing source. In one cool-region season a first-year plant yields more modestly, a handful to a couple dozen stalks depending on how early it was set out and how hot the summer ran.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One healthy clump can give you dozens of stalks by late summer, plus lots of leaves for tea. In warm, frost-free areas an established plant produces even more, year after year. In a short, cool season, expect a more modest first-year harvest.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Lemongrass starts slowly and only bulks up once real summer heat arrives, so the first-season harvest depends heavily on getting an early, well-rooted start into warm soil and feeding and watering it hard. In cold zones the biggest first-year lever is a head start indoors; a plant set out small into a short season stays small.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Lemongrass is slow at first and only takes off when it gets hot, so a first-year plant does best if you start it early indoors and then feed and water it well all summer. The earlier and warmer the start, the bigger the first-year clump.
factors_seasoned: Heat and sun: a warm, full-sun site is the single biggest driver of clump size; cool or shaded plants make few, thin stalks
Water: this high-demand grass needs deep, frequent watering to bulk up; drought thins the stalks
Nitrogen feeding: regular nitrogen-forward feeding drives the vegetative growth that produces harvestable stalks
Season length: frost-free zones grow a large perennial clump harvested year round, while short-season zones get one modest annual harvest
Head start: in cold zones, an early well-rooted start set into warm soil greatly increases first-year yield

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Moon-phase planting tradition assigns leafy, above-ground crops like lemongrass to the waxing phase between new and full moon. No Land Grant extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports a yield or quality benefit from moon-phase timing for lemongrass; the guidance is traditional folklore rather than a tested effect. It carries no advantage over simply planting within the crop's verified warm-season, frost-free window.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant browned or killed by cold
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Lemongrass is fully frost-tender. Foliage is damaged as temperatures fall toward 40 °F, and frost kills the top growth outright; a hard freeze can kill an unprotected in-ground clump entirely. The common mistake is planting out too early in spring or leaving the plant outdoors into fall frost. There is no recovery of frosted top growth, though a lifted or well-mulched crown may resprout in borderline zones.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Lemongrass cannot take cold. It gets damaged as temperatures head toward 40 °F, and frost kills the leaves. A hard freeze can kill the whole plant if it is left outside. The usual mistakes are planting it out too early in spring or forgetting it outdoors when fall frost comes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant out only after all frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed. In fall, harvest before first frost and lift and pot the clump (or a division) to overwinter indoors in bright light. In zones colder than about 8b, treat it as an annual or a keep-it-in-a-pot plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until frost is fully past and the soil is warm to plant it out. In fall, harvest before frost and bring a potted piece indoors for winter. In cold areas, plan to grow it in a pot you can move inside.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Few, thin stalks (too little sun or heat)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant is spindly with only a few stalks
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Lemongrass grown in shade, in a cool-summer climate, or without enough water and food produces only a few slender stalks and expands slowly; in deep shade it can decline and die. As a heat-loving grass it needs full sun, warmth, generous water, and regular nitrogen to build the dense clump that yields thick stalks.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Lemongrass in too much shade, a cool summer, or without enough water and feeding makes just a few thin stalks and barely grows. It needs full sun, heat, lots of water, and regular feeding to bulk up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Move it to the hottest, sunniest spot available, water deeply and often, and feed a nitrogen-forward fertilizer through summer. In cool-summer regions, grow it in a pot in a hot microclimate (against a south wall, on paving) and give it a head start indoors.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give it the sunniest, hottest spot you have, water it a lot, and feed it through summer. In a cool-summer area, grow it in a pot in a hot spot and start it early indoors.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Yellowing and rot from waterlogged soil
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant yellows and rots in soggy soil
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Despite its high water demand, lemongrass rots when its roots sit in waterlogged soil or a poorly draining pot. Symptoms are yellowing, wilting, and soft dark stalk bases even though the soil is wet. Drainage, not watering volume, is the failure here.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Lemongrass loves water but not soggy roots. If the soil or pot stays waterlogged, the plant yellows, wilts, and rots at the base even though it is wet. The problem is drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil; in containers use a free-draining mix with ample holes and empty the saucer after watering. Water generously but let the excess drain freely rather than pooling.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow it in soil or a pot that drains well. Water a lot, but make sure the extra water runs out and the pot never sits in a full saucer.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Lemongrass rust, caused by Puccinia nakanishikii, produces yellow flecks that redden into streaks and orange-brown pustules on the leaf undersides, drying the foliage in severe cases. It is the most notable disease of lemongrass in warm, humid regions and is worsened by crowding and prolonged leaf wetness.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Rust is a fungus that puts yellow flecks and orange-brown spots on the leaves and dries them out. It shows up in warm, humid weather, especially on crowded plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve airflow by spacing and dividing clumps, water at the base to keep foliage dry, and remove infected leaves promptly. Copper-based fungicides can be used preventively under heavy pressure. Full sun and vigorous, uncrowded plants resist rust best.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give plants room, divide crowded clumps, water at the base, and cut off spotted leaves. A copper spray can help if rust keeps coming back. Full sun and healthy, uncrowded plants resist it best.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Lemongrass is not a succession crop. It is a single perennial clump increased by division, not re-sown at intervals, so it is planted once and harvested from repeatedly. A gardener wanting more simply divides an established clump or roots additional stalks.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Start or root indoors 8 weeks before last frost; nursery start or rooted grocery stalk. Set out only after frost is past and soil warm.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Plant out about a week after last frost once soil has warmed. Lemongrass is frost-tender; do not rush it.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First stalks harvestable ~75-120 days after planting, once about half an inch thick.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Frost kills the top growth. Harvest heavily before first fall frost; lift and pot a division to overwinter indoors, or grow as an annual.

3.zone_notes: Zone 3 has the shortest warm season. Grow as an annual, or lift and pot a division before frost to overwinter indoors. A head start indoors is essential to get any harvest.

4.zone_notes: Zone 4 gives a short season. Start early indoors, plant after frost, harvest late summer, and overwinter a potted division indoors or treat as an annual.

5.zone_notes: Zone 5 supports a productive summer clump from a head-started plant. Overwinter a potted division indoors to reuse next year.

6.zone_notes: Zone 6 gives a good warm-season clump. Plant after frost, harvest midsummer into fall, and pot a division for indoor overwintering before frost.

7.zone_notes: Zone 7 has the longest northern_tier season. A clump set out in April can be harvested from June through fall. Lift and pot a division before frost to overwinter.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold-winter areas, grow lemongrass as a summer plant. Start it indoors about 8 weeks before your last frost (a grocery-store stalk rooted in water works great), then plant it outside once frost is past and the soil is warm. It stays small until it gets hot, then grows into a big clump. Feed and water it a lot. Start cutting stalks once they are about half an inch thick. Before fall frost, harvest a big batch, then dig up a piece into a pot and keep it in a sunny window over winter so you have it again next year.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, lemongrass is a warm-season annual bounded by frost. Start a division, nursery plant, or rooted grocery stalk indoors about 8 weeks before the last frost, then set it out a week or so after frost once the soil has warmed; it will sulk in cold ground. It grows slowly until summer heat arrives, then bulks up fast into a 3-to-6-foot clump. Feed it hard with a nitrogen-forward fertilizer and water deeply and often. Harvest stalks once they reach about half an inch thick, from midsummer into fall. Because frost kills the top growth, do a heavy final harvest before the first fall frost, and to keep the plant from year to year, cut it back, dig and pot a division, and overwinter it in a bright indoor window.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Start indoors ~8 weeks before last frost; South's long season lets it bulk up.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Plant out after last frost, spring, once soil is warm.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First stalks harvestable ~75-120 days after planting.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: In zone 8 frost ends the season; harvest before frost and lift a division indoors. In zone 9, mild winters may let the clump persist; protect or dig it in a hard freeze.

8.zone_notes: Zone 8 has a long, hot, humid season ideal for a big clump. Winter frost ends it; harvest before frost and overwinter a potted division, or protect the crown with heavy mulch.

9.zone_notes: Zone 9 gives a long harvest and often mild winters, so an established clump frequently overwinters as a perennial; dig or heavily mulch it if a hard freeze threatens.

10.zone_notes: Zone 9 gives a long harvest and often mild winters, so an established clump frequently overwinters as a perennial; dig or heavily mulch it if a hard freeze threatens.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Lemongrass loves the hot, humid Southeast and Gulf summers. Plant it out in spring after your last frost, then feed and water it well for a big clump. Harvest stalks from summer into fall. Because it is warm and humid, watch for leaf diseases: give plants room, divide crowded clumps, and water at the base. In zone 8, frost ends the season, so harvest before frost and bring a potted piece indoors. In zone 9, mild winters often let the plant come back year after year, but a hard freeze can still knock it back.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf's long, hot, humid summers are excellent for lemongrass, which thrives on the heat and moisture. Plant out in spring after the last frost and feed and water generously for a large clump by summer. Harvest stalks from early summer through fall. The one caution is disease: warm, humid, crowded conditions favor rust and leaf blight, so space and divide clumps for airflow and water at the base to keep foliage dry. In zone 8, winter frost ends the season, so harvest before frost and overwinter a potted division indoors or mulch the crown heavily. In zone 9, milder winters often let an established clump persist as a perennial, though a hard freeze can still cut it down.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Start indoors ~8 weeks before last frost.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set out transplants in spring after the last frost, once soil is warm.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First stalks harvestable ~75-120 days after planting.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Interior valley frost ends the season; harvest before frost and overwinter a potted division indoors.

8.zone_notes: Zone 8 interior valleys have hot, dry summers lemongrass loves and cold-enough winters to end the season. Harvest before frost; overwinter a potted division indoors.

9.zone_notes: Zone 9 interior gives a long, hot season and a big clump. Winter frost typically ends it; dig and pot a division to overwinter, or mulch the crown.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: California's inland valleys have the hot, sunny summers lemongrass loves. Plant transplants in spring after your last frost, then water deeply and often, since the dry heat makes the plant thirsty, and feed it well. Leaf diseases are rare in this dry climate. Harvest stalks from summer into fall. Winter frost ends the season inland, so harvest before frost and bring a potted piece indoors, or mulch the base heavily to try to keep it.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's interior valleys offer the hot, dry, sunny summers lemongrass thrives in. Set out transplants in spring after the last frost, water deeply and often (the dry heat drives high water use), and feed a nitrogen-forward fertilizer for a large clump. Dry-climate disease pressure is low, so rust and blight are seldom a problem here; the main task is simply keeping up with water. Harvest stalks from early summer into fall. Winter frost in the valleys ends the season, so harvest before frost and overwinter a potted division indoors, or mulch the crown heavily to try to carry it over.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Start indoors ~8 weeks before last frost; cool summers make a head start important.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set out in spring after frost; cool coast is marginal for this heat-lover.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Cool summers slow it; first stalks may take the full 100-120 days.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Cool coastal summers limit vigor; harvest before any frost, and in near-frost-free coastal pockets a clump may persist but grows slowly.

9.zone_notes: Zone 9 north coast is marginal: cool summers slow this heat-loving grass, so expect fewer, thinner stalks. A hot microclimate and a head start help. Overwinter a potted division indoors.

10.zone_notes: Zone 10 immediate coast is nearly frost-free but cool; a clump may persist as a low-vigor perennial. Grow in the hottest microclimate available (south wall, paving) for best results.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: The cool, foggy north coast is the hardest place to grow lemongrass, because it likes more heat than the coast usually gives. It will grow, but the clump stays smaller with thinner stalks. Give it the warmest spot you have, like against a sunny wall, and start it early indoors before planting out in spring after frost. Water and feed it well all summer. Right on the mild coast it may live through winter, but growth is slow; otherwise keep a potted piece indoors over winter.

Improve your odds by planting in the hottest microclimate you have (against a south-facing wall, over paving, or in a large dark pot that warms in the sun), giving a strong head start indoors, and setting out in spring once frost is past. fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, lemongrass grows all year as a perennial, since there is essentially no frost in zones 10 and 11. Plant or divide it any time (spring is best) in a sunny, rich, well-drained spot, and cut stalks whenever you need them. The thing to watch is not cold but disease: the humid, rainy summers can bring leaf diseases, so give plants room, divide crowded clumps, water at the base, and snip off spotted leaves. In the cooler winter weeks the leaves may turn reddish and growth slows, but the plant keeps going. Divide the clump every few years to keep it strong.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Florida's peninsula is warm and humid enough that lemongrass grows as a year-round perennial, with no frost boundary in zones 10 and 11. Plant or divide at any time, spring being ideal, in full sun and rich, well-drained soil, and harvest stalks in any month. The main management challenge is disease, not cold: the humid summer rainy season favors rust and leaf blight, so keep clumps open and divided for airflow, water at the base rather than overhead, and remove any spotted or streaked leaves. Foliage may redden and growth slow during the coolest winter weeks in zone 10, but the clump carries straight through. Divide established clumps every few years to keep the center productive.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Lemongrass is a tender, heat-loving grass, and the cool, foggy maritime Pacific Northwest is one of the harder regions to grow it well. Start a division indoors about 8 weeks before your last frost (a rooted grocery-store stalk works fine), then plant it out about a week after frost once the soil is warm. Give it your single warmest, sunniest spot, feed and water it well all summer, and expect a smaller clump with thinner stalks than gardeners in hot climates get. Before the first fall frost, harvest heavily, then dig up a piece into a pot and keep it in a bright window indoors over winter so you have it again next year.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Lemongrass is tender and heat-hungry, and the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, marine-tempered summer is a genuinely marginal climate for it: the region's long frost-free window gives this crop plenty of time but not the sustained warmth it wants. Site it in the single warmest microsite available (a south wall or over paving), feed it hard through summer, and expect a smaller clump with thinner stalks than a hot-summer garden produces, more so on the cooler immediate coast (z9) than the valley interior (z8). Harvest stalks once they reach about half an inch thick. Because frost kills the top growth, do a heavy final harvest just before the first fall frost, then dig and pot a division to overwinter indoors in a bright window; this crop will not survive the region's winter outdoors.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie, start lemongrass indoors in early February and set it out around April 1 after frost. It thrives right through the intense desert summer with no break, but it drinks heavily, so water deeply and often since the dry heat pulls moisture fast. Cut stalks from midsummer into fall. It cannot survive frost, so before the first freeze around November 1, bring a potted division indoors or somewhere sheltered to overwinter.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: USU Extension's suggested planting dates place St. George's frost-tender spring set at about April 1, following the March 30 average last frost; lemongrass is not one of USU's named Table 1 crops, so it rides that same frost-tender window, and it is well suited to the long Dixie summer ahead of it. Start divisions indoors in early February, about eight weeks before the April 1 set-out. The demanding input is water: deep, frequent irrigation at the base is essential in this heat. Harvest runs from midsummer into fall with no pause. Lemongrass is not frost hardy, so overwinter a potted division indoors or in a sheltered spot before the first freeze, around November 1.

description_seasoned: Lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus) is a tender tropical grass, a member of the true grass family (Poaceae), grown for the aromatic swollen white bases of its stalks and its lemon-scented leaves. Everything about its care follows from two facts: it is a warm-season grass that thrives on heat, full sun, rich soil, and abundant water, and it is frost-tender, damaged when temperatures drop toward 40 °F and killed outright by frost. It grows as a dense, non-running clump 3 to 6 feet tall, not a spreading runner like mint, so it stays where you put it and is increased by dividing the clump or by rooting a fresh stalk in water. In the tropics and frost-free zones it is a true perennial that can be harvested year round; across most of the country it is grown as a warm-season annual set out after the last frost, then either lifted and potted indoors before fall frost or replaced each spring. Because its own essential oils repel many insects, it is notably free of pest problems; rust and leaf blight are the diseases to watch in warm, humid, crowded plantings. Harvest by cutting whole stalks at ground level once they thicken to about half an inch; the tender inner stalk base flavors soups and curries, and the leaves make a fragrant tea.
description_beginner: Lemongrass is a tall, lemon-scented grass that loves heat, sun, rich soil, and plenty of water. It grows as a tidy clump, not a spreader like mint, so it will not take over your bed. It cannot survive frost, so in most of the country you plant it after your last frost and grow it through the warm months, then either dig it up and bring it indoors in a pot for winter or start fresh next spring. In the warmest, frost-free areas it can live outdoors year round. It is one of the easiest herbs to grow and is rarely bothered by insects, since its own lemony oils keep many pests away. To harvest, cut a whole stalk off at the base once it is about as thick as a pencil or thicker; the tender white bottom flavors cooking and the leaves make a lovely tea.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Begin harvesting once individual stalks have swelled to about half an inch thick at the base, which in a warm season is usually 75 to 120 days after planting a division or rooted start. Harvest a whole stalk rather than picking leaves: grasp an outer stalk, push it to the side, and twist and pull it free at the base, or cut it at ground level with a knife. Take the outermost stalks first and leave the clump intact to keep producing. Trim off the leafy top and peel away the tough outer layers to reach the tender inner base used in cooking; the fragrant leaves can be cut anytime for tea.
harvest_ready_beginner: You can start harvesting once a stalk is about half an inch thick at the bottom, roughly a few months after planting. Pick a stalk from the outside of the clump: bend it to the side and twist and pull it off at the base, or cut it right at ground level. Cut off the grassy top and peel away the tough outer layers to get to the tender white part for cooking. You can snip leaves anytime to dry for tea.
hardiness_notes_seasoned: Lemongrass is a tender tropical grass, reliably perennial only in essentially frost-free climates, roughly USDA zones 8b through 11, where established clumps persist and can be cut year round; foliage may redden and growth slows in the coolest winters of that range. Below about 40 °F the plant is damaged, and frost kills the top growth outright. In colder zones it is grown as a warm-season annual or, more often, kept in a pot that is moved indoors before frost and back out in spring, which lets the same clump live for years despite the cold.
hardiness_notes_beginner: Lemongrass only survives winter outdoors in the warmest, nearly frost-free areas (roughly zones 8b to 11). There it comes back year after year. Anywhere colder, frost kills it, so you either grow it as a one-season plant or keep it in a pot and bring it indoors for winter. Temperatures below about 40 °F start to hurt it, and a frost kills the leaves.

pet_safe.note: The essential oils can upset a cat or dog's stomach; large amounts can be more serious for horses.
